stemBlocks.value: In triangle OPQ, OP = 3u and OQ = v. Q is the midpoint of OR and M is the midpoint of PQ. L lies on OP with OL = (2/3)OP. (i) Write, in terms of u and v, an expression for a) LM and b) PR. (ii) Prove that L, M and R are collinear.
Think first: Q being the midpoint of OR means OR = 2v — that single line makes the collinearity fall out at the end.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p288-q11 from workbook page 288.

solutionSteps.instruction: Write OL and OR from the given conditions.

contentBlocks.value: OL = (2/3)(3u) = 2u; Q is the midpoint of OR so OR = 2 OQ = 2v

solutionSteps.instruction: Find OM using the midpoint rule on P and Q.
Subtract OL from OM to get LM.
Subtract OP from OR to get PR.
Form LR and compare it with LM.

contentBlocks.value: LR is a scalar multiple of LM and both start at L
Result: L, M and R are collinear

strategyBlocks.value: Write OL = 2u and OR = 2v, find M as the midpoint of PQ, then form LM and LR and show one is a multiple of the other.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: (i) a) LM = (1/2)(v − u) = (1/2)v − (1/2)u  b) PR = 2v − 3u  (ii) LR = 2v − 2u = 4 × (1/2)(v − u) = 4 LM. Since LR is a scalar multiple of LM and the two vectors share the point L, the points L, M and R lie on one straight line.

whyThisWorks.value: Two vectors that are scalar multiples of each other point along the same direction; if they also start at the same point, that direction is a single straight line through all three points. The rest is bookkeeping: the midpoint rule places M, the fraction 2/3 places L, and the midpoint condition on OR doubles v to reach R.

commonErrors.misconception: Using OR = v instead of 2v — Q is the midpoint of OR, not of OQ.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Using OR = v instead of 2v — Q is the midpoint of OR, not of OQ.

examTip.value: For collinearity, pick the two vectors that share a vertex (here LM and LR) — comparing LM with MR works too but the shared-point wording is cleaner.
